newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FEATURE - Nestle food labs hunt for breakthrough products.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Nestle food labs hunt for breakthrough products.

text.p: Ask to visit the Nestle Culture Collection at the giant food company's facility outside Lausanne and you won't see a wall full of Old Masters and Impressionists.

Instead you can survey a collection of some 4,000 pure strains of bacteria gathered over nearly three decades, many of them used for fermentation in Nestle factories around the world to turn perishable raw materials into stable cheese or dough.

The collection is the kind of thing white-smocked scientists boast about at the Nestle Research Centre, where the search is on for innovative products the company is counting on to tickle consumers' fancy and fuel sales growth.

The pressure is on to develop smash-hit products to follow Henri Nestle's original infant formula in 1867 and the bullion cube developed in 1886 by Julius Maggi, whose company Nestle swallowed 50 years ago.
Their dream is to find something to rival even Nescafe instant coffee, the product launched in 1938 that propelled Nestle into global prominence and changed the world's drinking habits.

"I can assure you that Nescafe, which lies some years back, will not be our last blockbuster," said Rupert Gasser, the Nestle executive in charge of production, technology, research and development. But he was tight-lipped on what that may be.
INNOVATION NOT ACQUISITIONS TO POWER GROWTH
Nestle bills the facility, where 600 people work, as the most important food lab in the world and the centrepiece of its global research network.
Research and development teams generate around a third of the new ideas that end up as Nestle products, with the quota in any given year ranging from 20 to 50 percent, officials say.
But new chief executive Peter Brabeck wants that to rise to around two-thirds as the company relies ever more on innovation -- not acquisitions -- to power sales growth.

He has taken personal responsibility for the company's new nutrition division, which develops and markets products ranging from infant formula to dietary supplements for the elderly to clinical foods fed by tube to very ill people.

People like Jurg Lechthaler now ponder the physical properties of pasta in the eternal search for convenience food that can cook up quickly but still has the same taste and consistency as traditional products.
"How do you keep the best spaghetti in the world from turning into clumps after five minutes on the table? This is not so easy," Lechthaler mused during a recent tour by reporters.
A wall chart showed how Nestle group researchers have discovered how to use thinner walls for pasta or to put grooves on noodles to speed up water diffusion during cooking.
Pasta experts at the Maggi group have attained more than 15 patents in the past three years, he said.

One patent covers using dried and filled pasta with at least one opening in the sealed periphery of the envelope for optimum results. High-tech, clover-shaped pasta gives the "mouth feel" of classical pasta after cooking for only five minutes.
"VIOLET STRAWBERRIES DON'T WORK"
Another scientist demonstrated the effect of lighting and colour on people's perception of food.
"Violet strawberries don't work. Would you eat violet strawberries?" he asked, demonstrating how food can switch from inviting to disgusting with a simple change of hue.

Others used a jar of pesto to demonstrate how controlled thawing of frozen basil leaves and a change in the length of heating during pasteurisation can improve a product's appearance without adding costs.

The labs brings together basic research and marketing to find ways to adapt Nestle products to local markets. The French, for instance, prefer darker coffee roasts and more robusta beans, while Germans like a lighter roast and more acidity.

The one cloud that hangs over the campus-like research facility is German-speaking Europe's resistance to embracing genetically-altered foods that the rest of the world seems to have accepted without another thought.
Nestle officials have insisted such products are safe, but the German-speaking market of nearly 100 million people in Europe has been putting up stiff resistance.
At the moment, Nestle does not offer any genetically altered products from its own research but sees them as a huge potential market.

"In any event, genetic technology will play an increasingly important role in the food sector. That is why we conduct basic research in this area here in Vers-chez-les-Blanc, to keep all options open for the future." Gasser said.
